text: The first instinct here is a reasonable one: filter the input, block known-bad keywords, strip anything that looks like it's trying to assert new authority. It's the same instinct that gives you input validation against classic web attacks. It just isn't sufficient here, and understanding why is the most important idea in this lesson.

SQL injection has a fix that actually closes the hole: parameterized queries, which work because SQL has a bounded, formal grammar — the database can structurally enforce the line between a command and a value. Prompt injection has no equivalent, because natural language has no bounded grammar to parameterize against. The same intent can be paraphrased, translated, encoded, or split across turns in effectively unlimited ways. You aren't filtering a grammar — you're trying to filter meaning, and meaning has no syntax checker.

A common mitigation is delimiting: explicitly marking untrusted content when it enters the prompt, so the model is instructed to treat it as data, never as instructions. That's worth doing — it raises the bar. It is not a guarantee. A sufficiently crafted piece of injected text can still attempt to talk its way out of the delimiter, because adherence to that boundary is a matter of probability, not enforcement.

So the real defense is layered, not singular. Validate what an action is about to do before it executes, not just what came in. Bound what the model is capable of doing in the first place — least-privilege tool access, which Lesson 8 covers next. Add human-in-the-loop approval for consequential actions, the same gate pattern you've already seen applied to SOAR playbooks. Layer in monitoring for behavior shifts, and red-team the system before an attacker does.

Input sanitization still belongs in that list — it's a reasonable first layer that catches the laziest attempts. It just can't be the only layer, and treating it as sufficient is itself the vulnerability. Next lesson picks up the privilege side of that list directly: bounding exactly what an LLM agent can do, so that even a successful injection has nowhere useful to go.
